rewrites.64EA31AA: Goal 1 carries most of the base case. Between 2025 and 2035 the base case adds 676,949 arrivals. The four hub markets, the UAE, Qatar, Ethiopia and Turkey, supply 206,584 of them and the mature markets 178,780. The acceleration markets, led by India and China, supply 175,818, regional Africa 110,298 and the strategic group 5,469. Conversion comes first and seats pace it at the peak, so the air access objective in Goal 2 runs beside this goal from the first phase (objective 7). The growth model's 1.8 million seat figure marks 2025 capacity (section 2.4). The goal is judged on arrivals by market group, foreign direct spend and green-season nights and share, not on arrivals alone (section 5.2).[^248]
rewrites.44CFE300: Yet two limits apply. The survey leaves out the domestic market and seven African markets, among them Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana. Its findings are directional rather than definitive, and no Western Cape validation exists yet. Stakeholders also name interests outside the four: medical tourism, township culture, eco-adventure and international business events. These are product interests that cut across the segments, not a fifth segment.[^253]
rewrites.4D7BAA88: The brand aim widens with it. Alongside conversion for the city, Wesgro should aim for recognition of the province's regions and for nights spent there. It should test brand presentations in market before fixing a hierarchy: Cape Town as gateway endorsement, a Western Cape umbrella and regional brands leading specialist campaigns. It should specify regional product, inventory links and completed regional bookings in campaign and airline agreements, which the April 2026 Emirates memorandum does not yet do.
rewrites.16C30FF6: The order matters. Segment targets and validation come first, in 2027, with the brand tests and a baseline of aided and unaided awareness for the city, the province and its regions (I16). The findings are directional, and Wesgro should not move the budget on them at scale until they hold for the Western Cape (section 4.3). Spend moves to each segment's own channels from 2028. Spend per visitor joins Wesgro's targets from 2029, once the data exists to track it.
rewrites.0DDE7511: Yet the trough is a seat problem as well as a demand problem. Airlines cut seats in the same months that visitors fall away, and connecting traffic is especially critical in the green season. Leisure marketing alone cannot fill a month that carriers have already thinned (section 2.4). The province needs reasons to travel that are fixed in the calendar, booked months ahead and sold with the seats.[^258]
rewrites.648E54D5: Green-season traffic has doubled since 2015, yet seats and rooms still trough from May to September, while international meetings peak from September to November.
rewrites.30BE356F: June to August and December to January are structurally weak for business events, and peak-date constraints lose events
rewrites.1E5053E9: Seats and visitors both fall away from April to September. International meetings run thin from June to August and peak from September to November, at the edge of the trough rather than in it. Events have one job: win new dates where seats and visitors are thinnest. May to August is the first portfolio, inside the April to September season.
rewrites.42891180: The record makes further growth credible without sizing it. Green-season traffic doubled in a decade, so weather alone has not fixed the size of the season. Yet winter rooms in Cape Town filled less in 2025 than in 2019 or 2023, so the task is recovery and conversion as much as promotion. No reading of the series credits a route, a campaign or an event for the gains.
rewrites.0AAFE38B: Two limits qualify the numbers. The October to March share is about 62% for 2025, computed from a month-of-travel table whose shares sum to 104.9% and normalised. The only reported split is 61% to 39% for 2024, and this report carries both. And only conferences are measured: meetings are absent from provincial statistics, incentive volumes are unverified and exhibitions are unquantified.[^260]
rewrites.0F2B24D4: Wesgro should build an April to September events spine and sell it with the seats, with May to August as its first winter portfolio. Its plan sets 161 business event bids over FY26 to FY30, and the spine decides when they land. Wesgro organises sales by buyer, because each buys differently: corporate midweek retreats, extensions to congresses already secured, new association bids, incentives with weather-resilient itineraries, exhibitions with non-local buyers and leisure events with non-local attendance. It contracts dated green-season offers for named low-demand weeks with airline and trade partners, with rain alternatives and buyer commitments before any public support. Incentive packages test the cooler season with Indian and Gulf planners.[^261]
rewrites.05307F88: The shared strategy and the count come first, in 2027. Wesgro agrees one event acquisition and calendar strategy with the Convention Bureau, the City and the Western Cape Government. The calendar strategy builds on the year-round promotion and business-events marketing in the City's framework for 2019 to 2024. Wesgro also sets up a way to measure meetings, incentives and exhibitions. It builds one monthly baseline of sold and available room nights, so that absolute winter nights and revenue are tracked beside the seasonal share. Without that count, no one can tell whether the calendar fills the trough. Wesgro then publishes the calendar and aims bids at May to August first (section 4.3).[^262]
rewrites.00079FAE: The evidence separates three kinds of product. Regional rooms are listed: every eligible case in the desk test had a platform listing, inside the core and outside it. Named attractions outside the core reach the marketplace as stops on Cape Town day tours, and none showed a standalone online ticket. Community product still sells by phone or through city operators (section 2.5).
rewrites.68D5E8DF: Wesgro should put the province beyond Cape Town where each market plans, with the information a traveller needs to commit. That means market-ready regional itineraries with transfers, opening seasons, safety information and a way to buy. Wesgro publishes them in the languages and on the platforms each priority market uses. Content comes first because it needs no new product. Wesgro builds it with the LTOs and the trade in 2027 and places it through the campaigns in objective 1 and the hub-market work in objective 4.
rewrites.6DF6EA15: Information turns interest the province has already earned into a plan, and a booking route turns the plan into payment. The Overberg says potential visitors do not grasp how close the district is to Cape Town. Content, listing and packaging go together. A listing puts outer-district product on the platform where a traveller already plans, but only visible, complete information reaches that traveller at the moment of decision. The audit then shows, district by district, which step fails and whether support moved it.[^269]
rewrites.6F2E7704: Yet both markets fell in 2026. Stats SA counted 37,875 tourists from India and 22,848 from China to South Africa from January to September, down 30.0% and 23.7%, after 69,680 and 37,902 in 2025 (section 2.3). Both markets had pilot access to the ETA before its August 2026 launch, so easier entry alone has not turned the trend.
rewrites.34C14ED5: About 71,000 travellers from India and about 30,000 from China reach Cape Town each year through Gulf and African hubs. They fly with carriers whose Cape Town business is built on onward traffic. Nine in ten of Qatar Airways' Cape Town passengers connect through its hub, as do more than 80% of Emirates'. Hub routes through Dubai, Addis Ababa and Doha run at load factors of 65.2% to 72.3%, so they have room for more.[^272]
rewrites.2A47F385: The 2026 decline changes the first step. Before activation spend rises, Wesgro and Cape Town Air Access run one diagnosis of both markets that sets routes, fares, entry and product side by side, with the hub carriers and the trade. It shows which brake binds in each market. Wesgro and Cape Town Air Access then test direct services commercially with carriers before any route case enters Phase 2, because stated interest is not a commitment.
rewrites.4F426FAA: The mature markets are where the province earns its premium. Its high-spend visitors come from Europe and North America, and the mature group grows steadily to 2035, but more slowly than the hub and acceleration markets (section 2.3). Growth here comes from value per visitor more than from volume.[^279]
rewrites.42C2A985: Value matters to the growth case because seats are scarce. Five mature long-haul routes already run above an 80% load factor: Newark, Atlanta, Frankfurt, Heathrow and Washington. The runway binds at the peak until relief arrives in about 2033 (section 2.4). Each extra rand per visitor on a full route is growth that needs no extra seat. Longer stays and travel beyond the Metro add value in the same way.[^280]
rewrites.40EE2836: Two things stand in the way: carrier pricing and the province's own measures. On full routes, carriers are expected to raise fares rather than add new services, which frustrates the wish for more visitors. The province must therefore earn more per visitor without losing share. Yet its targets count arrivals, and spend per visitor by market is reported for a single year.[^281]
rewrites.3D6E828E: The constraint is well documented; the lever is not. The five routes are full and their visitors pay most. Yet none of the work behind this report holds fare, revenue-per-seat or yield data. None models a yield uplift either. The yield lever rests on how carriers are expected to behave on full routes. This objective sets yield as an indicator to establish, not a target to hit, until spend per visitor by market is tracked every year. SA Tourism's 2025 figures by market are published, so the annual series can start (section 2.3).
rewrites.235C7DC3: The full routes come first. From 2027 Wesgro makes the frequency and gauge case to their carriers, because seats held now protect share until the runway relief arrives (section 4.3). Wesgro agrees the extension strategy with the US and UK trade in 2027, and luxury-advisor distribution follows in 2028. Spend per visitor and length of stay join Wesgro's own targets from 2029, once the data-sharing protocol supplies them (objective 18).
rewrites.71527488: Agree an extension strategy with safari and tour operators in the USA and the UK: two or three added nights in the Cape Winelands, on the Whale Coast or on the Garden Route, sold inside the itineraries they build
rewrites.1CEA444C: Africa is the province's nearest market and its steadiest: Namibia and Zimbabwe bring repeat and counter-seasonal demand. Regional trips are shorter in lead time and easier to convert, which helps the green season. Africa is both a base to keep and a market to grow (section 2.3).[^287]
rewrites.6BAB5929: Access is the constraint. Routes to Luanda, Maputo, Gaborone, Harare and Mauritius run above an 80% load factor, so added demand there meets full aircraft. Visas add friction. South Africa ranked 33rd of 54 African countries on the Africa Visa Openness Index, as the Western Cape Visa Regime Study reported in 2024. The CTICC also reports that regional African event demand is constrained by visa requirements.[^289]
rewrites.78DA6EA3: African demand is a Southern African volume base with two high-spending West African markets and regional routes above an 80% load factor.
rewrites.6D7CCD37: Kenya splits its demand in a similar way. Regional African markets drive its volume and business travel, while long-haul markets bring leisure demand and higher spend per visitor. It draws 41% of its arrivals from Africa, mainly from Uganda and Tanzania. Nairobi serves as East Africa's aviation, diplomatic and business hub through Kenya Airways' regional network. Kenya's arrivals grew 14.6% in 2024 to about 2.4 million, against world growth of 11%. The transferable changes are to treat business events as a system lever and to align city, provincial and national actors around one gateway strategy. The condition is seats and visas. Activation in Nigeria and Kenya converts only travellers who can get a visa and a seat.[^293]

inserts.text: Elsewhere the product itself is missing: the Overberg and West Coast marine and wildflower assets have no guided tours and no bookable product. What no source measures is the step after listing: whether the product is found, has inventory on the dates travellers want and converts into a sale. The I3 audit measures each step by district, for accommodation and for experiences separately, and sets the baseline for T2-04 (section 5.4).[^267]
